text:
The fluorescent hum of the Blackwood Bay archives was a lonely sound after closing, a thin solace against the deeper quiet. David Vance traced a finger across the smudged print of an old property deed, the ink bleeding into the cheap paper. Agnes Finch’s signature, a tight, nervous scrawl, sat next to a date stamped three weeks before her disappearance. The facts remained inert, refusing to yield a pulse, even as the building itself seemed to develop one.

A low thrumming began, a deep vibration that resonated up from the concrete floor, settling in the bones of the building and then in his own. It wasn't the distant rumble of a truck, but something more fundamental, a slow, methodical beat that carried a metallic tang into the stale air. His cheap portable radio, left on a low volume in the corner, hissed its usual static. Tonight, however, the white noise seemed to breathe, briefly coalescing into fragmented whispers, almost-words that dissolved before they could fully form, like a poorly-remembered echo trying to mock a conversation. He leaned closer, but it was gone, swallowed by the hiss.

He pulled his focus back to Agnes’s file, to the dead-end street names and the cryptic notes he’d made. Blackwood Bay always bled the real into the unreal, a constant, low-grade fever that skewed perception. The thrum beneath him, the spectral voices in the static – they were just background noise in this town, part of the landscape. But a good journalist knew even background noise could contain a signal, a rhythm that eventually led to a truth, no matter how unsettling.
